topic.title: Sanctuary cities
topic.proposition: Cities should limit their local police's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I recognize why people want tighter coordination, but I think it damages public safety when local police get pulled into federal immigration enforcement. If patrol officers double as immigration agents, immigrant residents will stop reporting crimes or serving as witnesses out of fear for their families. Community trust is the foundation of effective policing, and I think cities are right to keep that boundary between local law enforcement and federal immigration duties.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I understand that concern, but in my view the greater risk is letting jails release people who could pose a danger simply because a jurisdiction won't honor a federal request. When someone is already in custody for a serious offense, sharing that information with federal authorities seems like basic cooperation between levels of government, not surveillance of an entire community. Refusing to coordinate at that point strikes me as prioritizing symbolism over safety.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a reasonable worry, and I won't wave it away, but I think there's a meaningful difference between everyday policing and treating every jail booking as an invitation for federal involvement. Nobody is proposing that officers ignore violent crime. My point is that once immigration enforcement becomes entangled with routine arrests, including minor or later-dismissed charges, it sends a chilling signal to entire neighborhoods, making people afraid to interact with police at all, which undermines safety far more broadly.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I hear your distinction, but I think the safety costs of stepping back from cooperation are real and immediate, especially when someone with a serious record could simply walk free while a request goes unanswered. It's also worth remembering that federal authorities themselves have documented cases where local agencies chose not to honor these requests, regardless of the reasons behind those decisions. This is the claim I am relying on. Between 2014 and 2017 alone, ICE documented between 10,000 and 15,000 declined civil administrative detainers nationwide
